I'm going to be a bit more gentle, here, OP.

There is an ancient tradition called "pseudepigraphy" -- important books are attributed to important people, even if it's not true: "Moses" writes about his own death in the Torah, "Sun Tzu" describes warfare that resembles military science from about 200 years after his death, "Hermes Trismegistos" and other divine characters wrote many books, too. It's a really old tradition -- Egyptians were always reporting that writings about the gods were "found" in a tomb and the writing has been restored.

So, this is an important tradition. Consider all the Rosicrucian documents -- they tell us the story of Christian Rosenkreutz and how the books came to be revealed. But this story has as much occult significance as the books themselves. But how does this relate to the modern world?

First, you're right. Some crappy writers are just trying to heighten the drama. Consider Crowley, though. He invokes "Aiwass" even though people would have been willing to accept Crowley. And Crowley kind of admits that "Aiwass" was an "imaginary friend". I guess, "by their works shall ye know them"?

So, is it a valid rhetorical technique that is sometimes butchered? Maybe. But what about channelers and automatic writers -- all of Bahai was channeled if I remember correctly. Is it an external entity, or is some portion of the mind editing and recasting "truth" for the conscious mind? I don't know -- so I take it author-by-author.

At the other extreme, there are the authors who claim authorship but fake everything. I can understand why Waite obscured all the spells he edited -- he didn't want others doing "correct" spells. (That's a rabbit hole: can I reconstruct the "correct" spell if I know the theory? Can I create my own spell or do I need a revelation?) The ugly end of this is psychology. Both Jung and Freud misrepresented the details of the cases which formed their theories. I object to that, but I honestly think I would have objected less if they'd said "I communed with the spirit of Psyche before a scrying glass and she revealed the laws of human spirit." I mean, that's kind of a way of saying, "Well, I reflected on the matter abstractly..."

Now, I haven't read Ford, so it may be crap, but I'm not quick to judge, I guess.

Getting back to your original question, whIle I appreciate the reality of channeling, I tend to be skeptical both that people who claim to channel really are, and that even if they are channeling, does the spirit itself know what it is talking about? Obviously, if inspired worKs were all they were cracked up to be, there would not be a shitload of different, contradictory, and sometimes, simply, fucking crazy, religions in the world. Channeling seems like a cheap and easy way to claim superior knowledge.

I remember debating a point with someone when she said she was getting channeled information. I simply said "Thanks for sharing."; I was thinking "Don't argue with crazy." As I initially said, I do truly appreciate the potential reality of channeling, but am skeptical of claims.

I can think of 2 professional psychics who I feel are valid psychics, but I am skeptical of their commercialized channeling.
